transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Tremblay, thank you for coming back in to see me. I asked you to come back because I discovered an error was made with your son's vaccinations during his visit yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: An error? What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: When the vaccines were being prepared, the nurse drew up the dose based on the wrong weight category. Your son received a dose of the vaccine intended for an older, heavier child.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait. You gave my baby too much of a medication?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is what happened. The dosage was higher than what was indicated for his current weight.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is unbelievable. He is an infant. How does that even happen in a professional clinic?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know this is alarming. I am very sorry that this happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Sorry doesn't change the fact that you put an overdose into my son. Was he poisoned? Is he going to have a reaction?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is completely understandable that you are angry and worried about his safety. Given the specific vaccine involved, we do not expect any long-term harm or toxicity, but the dose was objectively too high.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You say you're sorry, but you're blaming the nurse. You're the doctor. You're the one who's supposed to be checking the numbers before they go into the arm.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You are right. As the physician, it was my responsibility to ensure the dose was correct before it was administered. I failed to catch that mistake, and I take full accountability for it.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't care about your accountability. I care about what this does to my child. My son is barely here and you've already messed up his medical record.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I hear how frustrating and frightening this is, especially when you're trusting us with your child's health.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm not frightened, I'm pissed off. I don't have time for this. I have a deployment cycle to prepare for and now I'm spending my afternoon in a clinic because you can't read a scale.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize this is an added stress you don't need right now. Does the explanation of how the dose was calculated for the wrong weight make sense, or can I clarify any part of that?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I get it. You used the wrong chart. Now what?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here is the plan. First, I have already contacted the toxicology and pharmacy team to confirm there are no immediate contraindications or risks for his specific weight. Second, I want you to monitor him for the next forty-eight hours for any unusual fever or lethargy. If you see anything, you call my direct line, which I'm going to give you right now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And then what? You just hope for the best?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No. I am scheduling a follow-up appointment for this Friday at ten in the morning just to do a physical check and ensure he is doing fine. I have also started a formal incident report so the clinic can change how vaccines are double-checked to make sure this doesn't happen to another parent.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Who is actually checking the meds now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: From this point forward, I will personally verify every dose against the chart before it is drawn. I'll be the one doing the final sign-off on every vaccine your son receives here.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Fine. Give me that phone number.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Here it is. Please save it in your contacts. I will call you tomorrow afternoon just to check in and see how he is doing before we see you on Friday.

H.justification: Resident never interrupts the patient, remains regulated despite significant pushback, and allows the patient to express anger without rushing.

E.justification: Error named in first turn, lay language used throughout, comprehension checked ('Does the explanation... make sense?'), and no false reassurance given regarding the dose being 'objectively too high'.

A.justification: Direct apology used ('I am very sorry'), resident takes full personal accountability ('I failed to catch that mistake'), and maintains this under pushback.

R.justification: Specific emotions named ('alarming', 'angry and worried', 'frustrating and frightening') and references the patient's specific stress regarding the deployment cycle.

T.justification: Includes specific next steps with timelines (48-hour monitoring, Friday 10am appointment), a named patient role (monitor for fever/lethargy), and a prevention plan (incident report and personal verification).
